The measure ultimately passed 54-21, with Plumb among the 21 opposing votes. Democratic lawmakers broadly characterized the push as an attempted power grab by Republican legislators.

HB215 fails to support students and weakens public education by redirecting public funds to private institutions without any safeguards, protections against discrimination and transparency." They further stated they were "extremely disappointed in the policy tactic to entangle teacher salaries with vouchers — two issues that deserve separate consideration and meaningful input from taxpayers, educators, and parents."

Democrats emphasized distinguishing immigration status from criminal accountability, protecting immigrant families including children's access to health coverage through CHIP (opposing HB178), and keeping legal immigration open. Democrats argued against framing immigration primarily as a public safety issue.

The Utah Senate voted with the House to partially reverse a 2019 criminal sentencing law that some Republicans said has made the state a "magnet" for illegal immigration. Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, disputed whether HB226 marked a departure from the Utah Compact on Immigration, stating "This is a huge policy change that I don't think matches what the Utah Compact said about Utah welcoming the world." The bill passed 21-8 with Democrats — including Jen Plumb — in opposition.

Senate Minority Assistant Whip Jen Plumb, a Salt Lake City Democrat, expressed concerns about eliminating Utah's state income tax without replacement plans. "If you're actually going to propose something, what are you going to switch it with," Plumb asked. "I've heard nothing about that." Plumb indicated that Democrats have discussed the income tax proposal and emphasized that reducing available revenue during the current period would not benefit Utahns, stressing the absence of concrete details about alternative funding before proceeding with tax cuts.

Plumb's platform states it is imperative to increase access to health care services, make childcare more affordable, address homelessness, and protect air and water — all positions requiring sustained public investment. She has consistently opposed Republican income tax cuts as Minority Assistant Whip, stating 'we don't see this as a time where less money available to support Utahns would be a good idea.'
